#4960. Bitcoin ETFs see another $570 million in net outflows as November total nears $5 billion and BTC dips below $60K

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs saw more than half a billion dollars in net outflows on Monday as bitcoin surrendered an Nvidia-fueled rally and slipped back below $60,000.

U.S. spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds saw another $569.7 million in net outflows on Monday as bitcoin surrendered an initial rally following the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia.

BlackRock's IBIT bitcoin ETF again led Monday's net outflows with $509.3 million exiting the fund, according to data compiled by The Block. IBIT's dominant bitcoin fund has recorded just one day of net inflows so far this month, with its cumulative November net outflows approaching $4 billion.

Grayscale's BTC and Bitwise's BITB also witnessed net outflows of $61.1 million and $12.6 million, respectively, while Fidelity's FBTC saw the only net inflows of $13.3 million. The remaining ETFs posted zero flows for the day, with the combined bitcoin ETFs nearing $5 billion in net outflows for the month.

Meanwhile, Ethereum ETFs also generated net outflows of $84.9 million on Monday, led by BlackRock's ETHA. U.S. Solana ETF saw a combined $3.8 million in net outflows for the day, while spot XRP ETFs recorded $2.5 million in net outflows, according to SoSoValue data.

Nicolai Sondergaard, senior research analyst at Nansen, argued that the selling represented a cyclical reduction in risk rather than a structural exit from bitcoin ETFs. Despite nearly $5 billion exiting the funds so far in November, cumulative net inflows remain around $52 billion, or about 83% of their October 2025 peak, he said.

However, Nansen data also shows little evidence that large holders are absorbing the ETF selling so far. Large wallets that rarely move coins received a net 10,000 BTC from exchanges over the past month, compared with approximately 70,000 BTC sold by ETFs during November, according to Sondergaard.

Bitcoin rose as high as $64,500 at one point on Monday amid a broad market rally following Nvidia's confirmation that it had reinstated Jensen Huang as president, CEO, and board director. Nvidia (NVDA) shares themselves closed up 31.5% at $165.06 on Monday, adding nearly $1 trillion in market cap, and are currently down 4.8% in pre-market trading on Tuesday, per TradingView.

However, Bitcoin Bitcoin (BTC) gave up its initial gains to finish Monday roughly flat before slipping back below $60,000 earlier on Tuesday morning. Bitcoin is currently trading for around $60,300, according to The Block's prices page.

Ether (ETH) witnessed a similar spike, but ended up trading down 0.8% for the day, while the GMCI 30 index, representing a selection of the top 30 cryptocurrencies, fell around 1.1%.

Joel Kruger, market strategist at LMAX Group, told The Block that elevated Treasury yields and continued expectations of an aggressive Federal Reserve policy path were keeping the dollar supported and making it harder for crypto to sustain a rebound.

#4959. Base makes quantum security a 2027 priority as regulators warn of risks

Base creator Jesse Pollak says the upcoming Everest upgrade will help prepare wallets for future quantum threats, although further changes will be needed.

Base, an Ethereum layer-2 blockchain developed by Coinbase, is making quantum security a priority for 2027 as it prepares to protect its network against future threats from quantum computers.

Base creator Jesse Pollak told Cointelegraph in an exclusive interview that the upcoming Everest upgrade will introduce a new type of transaction designed to lay the groundwork for quantum-secure wallets.

The network is the second-largest blockchain by decentralized finance (DeFi) total value locked (TVL), with approximately $5.1 billion in assets deposited across its protocols, according to DefiLlama.

The upgrade will not make wallets quantum-resistant right away, but Pollak said it is an early step toward introducing further protections in the future. “That doesn’t mean we’ll be able to solve all of it in 2027, but [it’s] something the team’s going to be working on,” Pollak said.

The plans come as global regulators warn that quantum computers could eventually break the security systems used across financial markets, including blockchain networks.

Quantum computers process information differently from regular computers and could one day allow hackers to access crypto wallets and steal funds. However, many experts have concluded that today’s quantum computers aren’t powerful enough to do this.

One of Base’s first steps will come through Everest, its upcoming fifth network upgrade. Pollak said the upgrade introduces a new transaction type called Base Transactions, which he expects to support future improvements to wallet security.

“That network upgrade doesn’t specifically solve quantum security for these wallets, but it does put in place the framework,” Pollak said.

The current technical specifications for Base Transactions, outlined in EIP-8430, still rely on existing cryptography rather than quantum-resistant signatures. However, the proposed transaction format separates how a transaction is signed from how its signature is verified, allowing the network to introduce new security methods in the future without requiring users to change their wallet addresses.

Base has not set a timeline for introducing quantum-resistant protections, beyond making the work a priority for 2027.

Related: Ethereum dev targets 2028 for quantum resistance, a year early

On Thursday, the International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO) warned in a report that sufficiently powerful quantum computers could threaten the security of financial systems.

The international regulator said blockchain networks could be especially difficult to protect because making security changes would require cooperation from many participants. It also warned that these upgrades could create new security problems, raise costs and disrupt transactions.

Meanwhile, advances in artificial intelligence (AI) could make cyberattacks harder to detect and analyze, the report notes.

Governments are also preparing for the threat, with the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) introducing its first three security standards designed to protect against quantum attacks in 2024, and releasing further guidance in October 2026. The agency has set 2035 as the primary target for completing the transition to quantum-resistant cryptography across US federal systems.

Beyond quantum security, Pollak outlined four priorities for Base in 2027: expanding trading, payments and lending, while preparing for a future in which AI agents carry out more financial transactions.

Pollak pointed to growing demand for tokenized stocks, saying weekly trading volume on Base had reached $1 billion. He said much of the interest came from investors outside the US seeking easier access to American stocks.

AI agents are also expected to play a bigger role in the network. “Agentic payments was a big trend in 2026. I think that agentic finance is going to be one of the biggest trends of 2027,” he said.

Base’s latest network upgrade, Denim, was rolled out on Nov. 5 and reduced block times from two seconds to 200 milliseconds, allowing the network to produce blocks 10 times faster.

The upgrade was followed by transaction delays on Base. Pollak said Base reviewed the incidents, made fixes and introduced additional testing to help prevent similar problems.

Looking ahead, Pollak said he wants future upgrades to happen without users noticing. “Our goal in 2027 is to make it so that upgrades are non-event. So no one’s even talking about them,” he said.

#4958. China's Z.ai Says Its New AI Model Can Think Like One Four Times Its Size

China's Z.ai Says Its New AI Model Can Think Like One Four Times Its Size

Chinese AI developer Z.ai released GLM-5.4 on Monday, introducing a new architecture that it claims delivers the reasoning capabilities of models nearly four times its size without requiring nearly as many parameters.

The Beijing-based company says its new 750-billion-parameter model can compete with systems containing two to three trillion parameters. It also supports a one-million-token context window, accepts images and video, and can generate up to 128,000 tokens in a single response, according to its technical documentation. Parameters are the internal values a model learns during training, while tokens are the chunks of text it processes and generates—roughly equivalent to words or parts of words.

The release comes as American companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google dominate the highest positions in AI performance rankings. Chinese developers, meanwhile, have increasingly focused on making powerful models cheaper to run, particularly for coding and autonomous agents.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Z.ai has been among China's strongest competitors. As Decrypt reported in August, its predecessor GLM-5.3 was already competitive with leading American coding models, although it still trailed the best proprietary systems on several software engineering tests.

GLM-5.4 introduces what Z.ai calls a Loop Transformer, which processes information through the same 28 neural network layers twice. Traditional Transformers generally pass information through each layer once, so reusing layers effectively increases computational depth without increasing the number of stored parameters.

The company combines this approach with gated updates, which regulate how much information changes between passes, and a hybrid memory cache that avoids storing an entirely separate copy of previous calculations. Sparse attention also helps the model focus its computing power on relevant information rather than processing everything equally.

In controlled experiments on a smaller 30-billion-parameter model, Z.ai reported that its looping technique increased accuracy on AIME 2025, a mathematics examination benchmark scored by the percentage of correctly solved problems, from 19.17% to 30.42%.

GPQA Diamond, a graduate-level science question-answering test also scored by correct-answer percentage, improved from 47.58% to 56.26%. The experiments required approximately 10% additional training compute, while reducing generated reasoning tokens by 10% to 14% on several tests.

Those results concern the experimental architecture, not independently established performance for GLM-5.4 itself. Z.ai has not published a comprehensive flagship benchmark comparison demonstrating that the new model matches Claude or GPT.

The company is also promoting what it calls Generalized Coding: using programming to accomplish tasks beyond software development. Its demonstrations include building a video game, creating 3D environments, and designing a six-axis robotic arm using engineering software.

The company's previous flagship costs $1.40 per million input tokens and $4.40 per million output tokens through its API. By comparison, OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Sol costs $2 and $10, while Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 costs $4 and $20, respectively.

At those published rates, GLM-5.3 is considerably cheaper than its American counterparts, although GLM-5.4's own API pricing has not been announced. Its actual performance-per-dollar advantage therefore cannot yet be calculated.

China has other serious contenders. Alibaba's Qwen 4 Max recently topped Chinese competitors on Arena's agent leaderboard, while Moonshot's Kimi K3 and DeepSeek V4 have challenged American developers on coding performance and API pricing.

The performance gap remains contested. A U.S. government evaluation placed DeepSeek roughly eight months behind the American frontier, although researchers questioned its methodology.

Z.ai itself remains on the U.S. Commerce Department's Entity List, following its January 2025 designation over concerns that its AI research could support Chinese military modernization. The restrictions limit access to controlled American technology, but have not stopped the company from releasing new models.

#4956. Crypto Market Structure Basics

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Exchanges, Liquidity, Orders, Derivatives, and Fundraising

Crypto market structure describes the venues, tools, participants, and settlement systems that allow digital assets to be bought, sold, priced, and transferred. It includes centralized and decentralized exchanges, order books, AMMs, trading pairs, market makers, derivatives, leverage, custody, and fundraising mechanisms.

Crypto markets offer a range of mechanisms and methods to trade crypto. Customers may choose to trade on centralized or decentralized platforms, and there are pros and cons associated with each. Here we look at the key components of the crypto market: the venues, actors, and financial products involved in driving price action.

We will consider the main features of crypto markets and what drives them, along with the various risks that traders should know about. Please note this piece is purely informative and should not be relied upon as a substitute for professional financial, legal or tax advice.

Below is a summary of the lessons in the course. For a detailed walk-through of each topic, please complete the interactive course.

Provides context around the range of venues, execution mechanisms, actors, products and associated risks in the crypto market.

Looks at the differences between CEXs and DEXs, and discusses order books, AMMs and liquidity pools.

Lesson 2 - Crypto Trading Pairs and Settlement

Describes the base and quote currencies within a pair, and the difference between on- and off-chain trade settlement.

Introduces the primary order types used to trade crypto (i.e. market, limit, stop, etc.) and some additional terms to be familiar with.

Lesson 4 - Longs, Shorts and Borrowed Exposure

Discusses the notion of going long or short crypto, using margin and trading on perpetual futures products.

Lesson 5 - Risks Associated with Derivatives

Considers the implications of highly leveraged positions and the impact of futures and options on the wider market.

Lesson 6 - Further Market Actors and Risks

Explores some of the other key market participants and additional forms of market abuse.

Presents an overview of the role played by VCs, PEs and alternative fundraising techniques in the crypto sector.

As mentioned above, crypto can be traded via either Centralized or Decentralized Exchanges.

As their name suggests, CEXs provide a service akin to a standard trading account. Customers will typically hold crypto with the CEX, which provides a venue to facilitate trades. In doing so, CEXs bridge the gap between one or more blockchains and their end-user base.

Alternatively, with DEXs, customers generally do not need to transfer their crypto into a centrally managed exchange account. Trading can take place directly from the customer's own wallet, most commonly facilitated via smart contracts.

Once we step away from the distinction between CEX and DEX, there are several mechanisms to bring together demand and supply for a given asset. Most obviously, many crypto exchanges will operate an order book. Users submit orders specifying the price at which they wish to purchase or sell the relevant asset. When compatible buy and sell orders are available, the exchange can match them and execute a trade.

A second approach is seen on many DEXs, where an AMM is employed. Liquidity pools comprise crypto assets deposited into smart contracts. When a user wishes to transact against these, they interact with the pool, at a price dictated by a mathematical function and the available liquidity.

Similar to FX, crypto is quoted in terms of a pair. For example, if someone buys the BTC/USDT pair, they will receive BTC and pay in USDT. BTC is the base currency and USDT is the quote currency, meaning the pair's price expresses how much USDT is required to purchase one BTC. Once a customer understands the composition of a trading pair, they will know what currency they are acquiring, giving up and at what price.

Finally, we must distinguish how a trade will be settled. CEXs typically maintain internal ledgers of their customers' holdings and execute trades without recording each transaction on the blockchain. On-chain transfers generally occur when assets enter or leave the exchange, while trades within the platform can be processed internally. On many DEXs, trades are executed and settled through smart contracts on the relevant blockchain, although parts of the order-matching or routing process may happen off-chain. The former approach will therefore tend to offer greater speed, whereas on-chain settlement is subject to the throughput and cost of the underlying blockchain.

Three common order types form the basis of the language used by crypto traders. A 'market' order instructs the platform to buy or sell immediately at the best available prices, although the final execution price will depend on available liquidity. With a 'limit' order, the trader specifies the maximum price they are willing to pay or the minimum price they will accept. Finally, a 'stop' order triggers another order once a certain price threshold is reached, although this does not guarantee execution at the trigger price.

There are further terms that traders will come across to denote their typical style of trading, such as 'scalping', 'swing' or 'buy and hold'. Again, these are simply descriptive and should not be construed as prescriptive.

A natural extension of the discussion above is that customers can take long or short positions on a crypto asset. Going long means taking a position that benefits if the asset appreciates in value, often by purchasing it directly. Conversely, a short position enables a trader to profit from a decline in the asset's price, although losses can arise if the price moves in the opposite direction.

By using borrowed funds or margin, a customer can increase their exposure beyond the capital they initially commit. While this can lead to greater returns, it also magnifies potential losses. Perpetual futures ('perps') are another product designed to allow traders to take exposure to the future price movements of an asset without a fixed expiry date. These use periodic funding payments between long and short positions to help keep contract prices aligned with the underlying market. Depending on the funding rate and their position, traders may either pay or receive funding.

If a large proportion of the market is exposed to high levels of leverage, the likelihood of forced liquidations can increase during sharp price movements. In turn, the buying or selling triggered by these events may place further upward or downward pressure on the market, potentially creating a liquidation cascade. Futures and options can provide a degree of protection when used to hedge existing exposures (and can of course be used to increase speculative exposure). However, they too carry considerable risk.

It will be apparent from the preceding discussion that customers require access to sufficient liquidity in order to efficiently enter and exit positions. On CEXs, market makers play an important role by submitting buy and sell orders, helping to maintain liquidity and reduce spreads. Similarly, many DEXs depend upon third parties supplying crypto to their liquidity pools, in return for a share of the trading fees generated.

There are a number of further considerations relating to the operation of crypto markets. Some of the more prominent forms of market manipulation are:

And finally, there are a number of other actors and entities that play a part in the crypto market: crypto custodians, information aggregators, government and supervisory authorities, and ETF issuers.

Finally, we touch upon some of the ways in which crypto businesses can secure finance. As with any industry, venture capital (VC) and private equity (PE) firms can invest in crypto-related ventures and provide a range of services beyond pure capital injection. Furthermore, there has been significant innovation in how crypto-native businesses can access funding. The sale of a project's native token(s) can occur via an ICO, allowing it to raise capital through token distribution. The advent of DEXs and CEXs has also enabled IDOs and IEOs respectively. In some cases, groups of investors can coalesce to form a DAO to collectively raise and deploy funds.

There are a number of key elements to understand in order to navigate the crypto market, spanning the range of venues, execution and settlement mechanisms, market actors and financial products.

Both CEXs and DEXs are capable of supporting customers, but differ materially in respect of custody and transparency.

Order books match compatible buy and sell orders, while AMMs use liquidity pools and algorithms to determine trading prices.

The decision to settle trades on- vs. off-chain will have material implications for customers.

Customers can use borrowing or derivatives to build larger positions, and the prevalence of leveraged exposure can create feedback loops throughout the market.

A diverse set of organizations underpin the crypto market, and will continue to evolve over time.

Lastly, the range of fundraising avenues open to crypto businesses also warrants careful consideration.

Market structure: The various mechanisms, market actors, products, rules and economic incentives governing the trading and pricing of an asset.

Centralized Exchange (CEX): A platform that facilitates trading and will typically hold customer assets or balances in custodial accounts.

Decentralized Exchange (DEX): A platform or protocol that enables customers to conduct trades directly from their wallets, commonly through smart contracts.

Order Book: Records the current set of outstanding bids and offers, allowing compatible buy and sell orders to be matched.

Bid: The price a buyer is willing to pay for an asset.

Offer: The price a seller is willing to accept for an asset.

Automated Market Maker (AMM): Allows trading against a pool of assets, with prices determined by a predefined algorithm.

Liquidity: The capacity to transact in an asset without materially affecting its price.

Slippage: The extent to which a trade's execution price differs from the anticipated price.

Settlement: The process of completing a trade and transferring or recording the resulting asset ownership or balances.

Leverage: The use of borrowed funds or derivatives to increase a customer's market exposure relative to their committed capital.

Perpetual Future: A futures-style instrument that does not have a fixed maturity. Generally uses periodic funding payments to help align its price with the underlying market.

Funding Rate: The rate used to calculate periodic payments between long and short positions in perpetual futures markets. Depending on the rate, either side may pay or receive funding.

Liquidation: The forced closing or reduction of a leveraged position when its available margin or collateral falls below the required threshold.

Market Maker: A firm or entity that provides buy and sell quotes to a market, helping maintain liquidity.

Initial Coin Offering (ICO): A fundraising mechanism through which a project offers tokens to participants in exchange for capital.

Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO): A structure allowing members to take collective decisions based on governance rules, which may include token-weighted voting.

A CEX is an intermediary platform that usually holds user balances, while a DEX lets users trade from their own wallets through smart contracts.

An order book lists bids from buyers and asks from sellers. When prices align, a trade can execute.

An AMM is a smart-contract mechanism that lets traders swap against a liquidity pool instead of a traditional order book.

Leverage increases the size of a position using borrowed funds or derivative exposure, which can amplify both gains and losses.

A perpetual future is a derivative contract without a fixed expiration date, usually kept near the spot market through funding payments.

#4955. BTCS offloads $44M in ETH to reduce DeFi debt amid market downturn

BTCS sold more than half its Ether holdings to reduce leverage following the market sell-off, while BitMine added another 7,819 ETH to its treasury.

Nasdaq-listed blockchain company BTCS sold approximately 27,300 Ether on Friday to repay $43.8 million in loans on decentralized lending protocol Aave as cryptocurrency markets plunged.

According to a Monday filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission, BTCS sold the Ether (ETH) on Nov. 20 and used the proceeds to reduce its outstanding Aave debt to approximately $10.5 million.

The transaction reduced BTCS’s Aave borrowings by approximately 81%, as the company sought to limit liquidation risk amid heightened market volatility. Its remaining Aave positions had a loan-to-value ratio of approximately 32% following the repayment.

BTCS reported approximately $17.9 million in outstanding convertible notes, in addition to its remaining Aave borrowings, according to the company’s announcement. The company also said it temporarily exited liquidity pool positions in its Imperium DeFi business as part of its efforts to reduce exposure to further market volatility.

Following the sale, BTCS held approximately 24,245 ETH, with cash and digital assets valued at a combined $61 million as of Sunday. The 27,300 ETH sale represented approximately 53% of its combined pre-sale ETH holdings.

The move follows a similar reduction in Ether exposure by digital asset manager CoinShares, which disclosed last week that it sold its entire ETH treasury position and half its Solana (SOL) holdings in October to fund share buybacks.

Related: Bitmine edges toward 5% of ETH supply as treasuries report buys amid market slump

Meanwhile, Tom Lee’s BitMine Immersion Technologies continued accumulating Ether, purchasing another 7,819 ETH over the past week despite the market downturn.

According to a Monday announcement, BitMine now holds 6,085,564 ETH, representing 4.98% of the cryptocurrency’s total supply. The company said it has purchased Ether every week since adopting its treasury strategy in June 2025.

BitMine also reported $384 million in cash and marketable securities as of Sunday. The company has staked approximately 5.23 million ETH, representing 86% of its total Ether holdings.

BitMine accounts for roughly 75% of the Ether held in corporate and government treasuries tracked by CoinGecko, which listed 35 entities holding a combined 8.16 million ETH at the time of reporting.

The contrasting strategies come as Ether continues to struggle, trading at approximately $1,743 as of 6:35 p.m. UTC on Monday, down 37.7% over the past year and 24.8% over the past 30 days, according to CoinGecko data.

Trump Says He 'Made the Deal' to Reinstate Jensen Huang, Sparking Bipartisan Backlash

U.S. President Donald Trump has taken credit for Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia, drawing criticism from lawmakers in both parties who say the administration has yet to explain what assurances it gave the company's board.

"I convinced them," Trump told CNBC in a phone interview on Monday, shortly after Nvidia reinstated Huang as president and CEO. "I made the deal."

Trump said the board had asked for assurances that Huang was not a national security threat, and that the administration provided them based on "everything we know." He said a government investigation had found that Huang himself was exonerated. Asked whether last week's stock losses had shaped his view, Trump said "probably so."

The board's decision was sealed by a personal promise from Trump on Sunday, CNBC reported, citing three people familiar with its thinking. Senior administration officials had contacted directors overnight on Friday, and Huang then joined meetings with the board over the weekend, the outlet said. The board's statement cited input from "senior levels of the United States government" without naming anyone.

Attorney General Todd Blanche told Trump and Vice President JD Vance on Saturday that Huang was not the target or subject of any Justice Department investigation, and that there was no evidence he had broken laws, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing U.S. officials.

During a marathon board session on Sunday, Huang disclosed additional affairs beyond the two that had been widely reported, but was contrite, the newspaper said, citing people familiar with the discussion.

Trump told The New York Times that he had consulted Blanche and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton before recommending Huang's return. "I had to go to them before I recommended this," he said. A day earlier, Clayton had said that the U.S. investigation into Alice Huang and her former company, Megaspeed, was ongoing.

The reversal came six days after board chair Harvey Jones said directors did not intend to bring Huang back. Trump later posted an AI-generated image on Truth Social showing Huang holding a red bra aloft in his raised fist, in a pose modeled on the photo of Trump after the 2024 assassination attempt on his life.

Huang's reinstatement drew the ire of lawmakers on both sides of the aisle.

"The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers," Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), ranking member of the Senate Banking Committee, said in a statement. She called on the administration to explain what input was given, and by which officials.

Republicans also pushed back. Sen. Tom Cotton (R-AR), chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, tweeted that the controversy over Nvidia and Megaspeed was "not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back," and pledged to pass chip export-control bills including his Chip Security Act.

I have warned the administration from the start about Communist China obtaining our most advanced chips through both smuggling and remote access. The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it’s not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back.…

— Tom Cotton (@SenTomCotton) November 23, 2026

"No national security risk? Based on what?" Sen. John Cornyn (R-TX) tweeted, quoting the board's statement. Sen. John Curtis (R-UT) asked who in government had weighed in and what they told the board, noting that it had ruled out Huang's return only a week earlier. "I'd like to know what changed," he wrote.

Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-NE) tweeted that Huang's behavior "does not support reinstatement," adding that Nvidia still had to answer for national security concerns and "unaccounted-for chips."

Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY), who is expected to become House Speaker in January, called the board's decision "indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible" in a statement. He promised an investigation into Nvidia and into what he called "corrupt abuse of power" by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and his department.

Trump's own Nvidia holdings may have gained as much as $15 million in value on Monday, according to the Financial Times, which calculated that he could have held up to 370,000 shares as of September 30, based on his latest ethics disclosure. At the low end of the disclosure's ranges, he would have held about 32,000 shares and gained $1.3 million. The White House did not respond to the newspaper's request for comment.

Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-AZ) tweeted that the president was "selling out our national security to keep the stock market high," calling for an investigation into stock trades made before the announcement.

Nvidia shares closed up 31.5% at $165.05 on Monday, adding about $950 billion to its market value, before slipping 5% to $156.82 in premarket trading on Tuesday, according to Yahoo! Finance.

Huang is due to sit for a closed-door interview with three House committees on December 1, and to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on December 3. On Monday, the Commerce Department also added Megaspeed to its Entity List trade blacklist.

#4950. Kalshi secures temporary win in New York gambling law dispute

The ruling allows Kalshi to continue operating as its legal battle with New York over sports-related event contracts moves toward a January hearing.

A New York state court judge on Monday denied the state attorney general’s request for a temporary restraining order against prediction market operator Kalshi, allowing the company to continue offering event contracts in New York as a legal battle over its sports-related markets proceeds.

In a statement to Cointelegraph, Elisabeth Diana, Kalshi’s head of communications, confirmed the ruling, saying the judge recognized the complex legal questions surrounding derivatives and federal preemption.

“The judge denied the State’s request for a TRO, recognizing that there are complex questions about derivatives and preemption. We remain committed to working with the State on a path forward that works for our 1.5 million customers and for the state of New York,” Diana said.

The denial of the temporary restraining order does not resolve the broader dispute over whether Kalshi’s federally regulated event contracts are subject to New York’s gambling laws.

The case will now proceed toward a preliminary injunction hearing set for early January, when the court will consider whether to restrict Kalshi’s event-contract operations in New York. Before then, both parties are scheduled to return to court on Nov. 30 to discuss potential restrictions on users aged 18 to 20, following concerns raised by the judge over the state’s minimum legal age of 21 for sports betting.

Related: CFTC halts some Kalshi Trump mention markets over manipulation concerns

New York sued Kalshi in July, alleging the prediction market operator was running an illegal, unlicensed gambling business by offering event contracts tied to sports, elections and other outcomes. The lawsuit seeks to halt the company’s operations in the state, recover alleged illegal gains and impose civil penalties.

The case followed an October 2025 cease-and-desist order from the New York State Gaming Commission, which prompted Kalshi to challenge the state’s authority in federal court. Kalshi argues that its status as a federally regulated derivatives exchange places its event contracts under the jurisdiction of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC).

In August, the CFTC warned that New York’s requested restraining order could prevent Kalshi from offering event contracts nationwide because the exchange is based in the state. The regulator also said New York was seeking more than $36 billion in damages.

In a separate federal court proceeding on Friday, US District Judge Lorna Schofield rejected the CFTC’s emergency request to block New York from pursuing its enforcement case against Kalshi, according to Reuters.

Kalshi isn’t the only prediction market operator facing legal action in New York. The state also sued Polymarket in September over allegedly offering illegal sports betting contracts, following similar actions against platforms operated by Coinbase and Gemini in April.

#4947. Coldcard Postmortem Says Weak Seeds, Not Hacked Devices, Drove Bitcoin Thefts

Coinkite on Tuesday published its full postmortem on the Coldcard seed-generation flaw that let thieves drain bitcoin from customer wallets starting in July, saying no device was hacked and that the stolen keys were rebuilt offline from weak seeds.

The 18-page report, dated Nov. 23 and modeled on a National Transportation Safety Board accident report, lays out how the defect shipped in Coldcard firmware from March 29, 2021, through July 30, 2026, and why years of outside reviews missed it.

“The losses are real and, for some customers, life-changing. No report or firmware update can undo that. We are sorry,” Coinkite wrote.

A seed is the list of recovery words that controls a bitcoin wallet, and it is only as safe as the randomness used to create it. Coldcard devices were supposed to draw that randomness from the hardware random number generator built into their STM32 chip.

Instead, a firmware setting switched that hardware source off, and a safeguard in Coinkite’s libNgU code library failed to catch it. Seed generation quietly fell back to Yasmarang, a predictable software generator built into MicroPython, the programming environment the firmware runs on.

Nothing crashed, and the devices produced normal-looking seed words. Coinkite estimates affected seeds carried roughly 40 bits of effective security on the older Mk2 and Mk3 models and about 72 bits on the Mk4, Mk5 and Q, against an intended 128 bits. That shrinks the pool of possible seeds enough for attackers to search it offline.

The report says Coinkite’s release checks confirmed the hardware code was present, but never confirmed that seed generation actually reached it. At least 15 independent review efforts since 2021 also missed the flaw, including two paid third-party reviews and an AI-assisted firmware review this year that produced 85 candidate findings.

Unexpected transactions from affected seeds began July 29. Coinkite said it identified the defect the next day, after users discovered thefts, and shipped fixed firmware for every supported release track on July 31.

As of Nov. 18, Coinkite had received about 300 loss-related support tickets tied to 242 customer accounts, or about 0.21% of its estimated Coldcard user base. The company’s blog post cites 236 accounts. Because Coldcard is self-custodial, Coinkite can only count losses that customers report, and it says the true number is likely higher.

The report cites Galaxy Research figures showing 1,778.84 BTC stolen from more than 8,600 addresses, worth about $107 million at today’s price. Galaxy pegged losses above $115 million in August, based on prices when the coins were taken, and white hats later moved some exposed coins into a recovery trust.

Who found and exploited the flaw is still unknown, and law enforcement is investigating. The report calls AI-assisted discovery “a plausible hypothesis, not an attribution,” noting that the first thefts came two days after the full model weights of the AI model Kimi K3 were released. Bitcoin Core developers ended long embargoes last month for bugs that AI tools can easily rediscover.

Coinkite said an independent review by Keylabs, published Oct. 15, found the defect “fully closed” in Mk5 firmware 5.6.2 and 5.6.3 and Q firmware 1.5.2Q and 1.5.3Q. That review did not cover Coldcard’s Edge releases, a preview track for developers and early adopters.

Newer Coldcard firmware now requires users to add their own randomness, through key presses, dice rolls or coin flips, and mixes it with three hardware sources. The device also checks at startup that seed generation reaches the hardware generator, and stops if it does not.

But a firmware update does not repair a seed that was already created on affected firmware. Coinkite told owners whose seeds were made on affected firmware to install verified fixed firmware, create a new seed and move their coins. Seeds made with at least 50 private dice rolls were not weakened.

Three of the report’s 15 recommendations to Coinkite remain open, including whether to compensate affected customers. The company said it has “no decision” on a plan yet and asked whoever holds the stolen bitcoin to return it through [email protected].

#4946. US seeks to recover $1.1B in crypto stolen in North Korea-linked Binance hack

US prosecutors are seeking control of stolen USDC, while Elliptic says hackers have moved $247 million through Bitcoin mixers.

The US Department of Justice is seeking to recover more than $1.1 billion in crypto stolen from cryptocurrency exchange Binance in October by hackers linked to North Korea.

In a court filing Monday, prosecutors asked a federal court in Washington, DC, to permanently forfeit the funds, which are held in USDC – a stablecoin issued by Circle. The filing follows a court order obtained earlier this month allowing authorities to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion in assets linked to the hack. Since the attack, which occurred on Oct. 29, US authorities said they have helped to freeze, seize or return nearly $3 billion of the more than $6 billion taken from Binance.

“Following the Binance theft, the FBI and our partners moved quickly to trace and freeze stolen assets and share critical information with virtual asset service providers,” said in a statement Brett Leatherman, operations director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s (FBI) cyber branch.

Binance has also pursued legal action to recover the stolen assets. On Nov. 18, the exchange said it had secured a $6.5 billion worldwide freezing injunction from the Abu Dhabi Global Market Courts. The orders target unidentified attackers and allow legal notices to be delivered through blockchain transactions to wallets linked to the theft.

The filing comes as blockchain analytics firm Elliptic also reported an analysis updated Monday that hackers had moved at least $247 million in Bitcoin (BTC) through crypto mixers – tools that make stolen funds harder to track. The firm said another $2.22 billion remained in wallets linked to the theft, while $2.85 billion had been frozen or seized.

Elliptic noted that hackers had moved stolen funds through more than 27,000 wallets across at least 16 blockchains. However, most of the crypto had not yet been converted into cash, and the 18,270 BTC stolen directly from Binance had not moved since the attack.

US authorities have linked the attack to a North Korean hacking group called TraderTraitor. According to Binance, the hackers gained access to its systems after tricking an employee into downloading malicious software. Following the attack, Binance said it had committed more than $6.34 billion to cover the losses and reassured that customer funds were safe.

#4945. $14.7B in ‘Lost’ Bitcoin Has Moved Since 2018: Report

$14.7B in ‘Lost’ Bitcoin Has Moved Since 2018: Report

Bitcoin that hasn't been moved in years is sometimes considered "lost" by industry onlookers, and one lawsuit is arguing that they've been "abandoned." But since 2018, roughly 10,000 supposedly lost Bitcoin wallets have sprung back to life.

Pseudonymous developer Quickben22 built a list in 2018 of 92,076 Bitcoin wallets that hadn't moved funds in more than six years, assuming the owners had lost their keys. Eight years later, the developer revisited the list to discover that 9,990 of those wallets have since moved a total of approximately 245,000 BTC, or just over $14.7 billion at Bitcoin's current price.

"Dormant is not the same as lost," Quickben22 told Decrypt. "I expected nearly all of the 92,076 addresses to still be silent after 8 years. About 89% are, but 9,990 have moved, and 14+ year old addresses are still waking up."

That distinction matters, as the findings come as a New York lawsuit brought by a pseudonymous plaintiff known as 'Noah Doe' tries to claim 39,069 dormant Bitcoin addresses as abandoned property, including wallets linked to Bitcoin creator Satoshi Nakamoto.

The plaintiffs argue the coins are "abandoned" under New York's lost property law. They say they found the wallets, reported them to the NYPD, and sent the owners notice by attaching on-chain messages to tiny Bitcoin transactions.

"It's like writing down the addresses of every locked house on a street, telling the police, and claiming whatever is inside because nobody answered the door," Quickben22 said.

Some wallets linked to the suit have since woken up, with several moving funds earlier this year—including one first funded in 2013 that shifted 411.45 BTC in October, then worth $33.4 million. One pseudonymous holder has also filed a motion to dismiss the case, claiming to still control a named wallet.

Quickben22's list was originally built for an app called Bitcoin Key Hunter, which guesses private keys at random and checks them against the dormant addresses in the hope of landing on one.

"It's like playing the lottery, but with much, much smaller odds," he said, before breaking down the math: roughly 1 in 10^43 across the whole list. "Those are about the odds of winning five Powerballs in a row," he added.

Quickben22 did not respond to Decrypt's query on whether he has successfully guessed the keys to any of the listed wallets.

It is impossible to know who exactly moved the funds from the supposedly lost wallets—it might not even be the original owner. An original owner tidying up old funds looks the same on-chain as someone who found a seed phrase in a drawer, or a hacker who got hold of a key that was never theirs.

"The blockchain shows that someone could sign, but not who," Quickben22 wrote.

Even when a wallet really is lost, the owner doesn't always let go.

Welshman James Howells has spent more than a decade trying to recover a hard drive holding around 8,000 BTC, which his then-girlfriend accidentally threw out during an office clear-out in 2013. He traced it to a landfill in Newport, Wales, and spent years seeking permission to dig it up, until a judge dismissed his case on environmental grounds. Howells called the ruling a "stitch-up."

Last year, he offered the local council £2.5 million to buy the landfill outright, Decrypt reported. The council didn't respond. He has since given up the search and is instead launching Ceiniog, a Bitcoin layer-2 network with a token he says is backed by the buried coins he can't access.

“MY view is this: As long as YOU (or anyone else in the world) can view the balance [and can] verify for yourself that it still contains 8,000 Bitcoin, then [the] Ceiniog coin is fully backed with its value,” he told Decrypt last year. “If those coins ever moved, Ceiniog instantly loses its backing and value. I am guaranteeing that those coins will never move—because the private key is on a [hard drive] in a landfill.”

Howells' 8,000 BTC haven't moved since 2013. On paper, they look exactly like the coins on Quickben22's list, and the kind the Noah Doe lawsuit wants declared abandoned.

#4942. CFTC staff say exchanges can count Bitcoin toward operating reserves

The staff guidance allows Bitcoin, Ether and payment stablecoins to count towards operating reserves.

US Commodity Futures Trading Commission staff said Monday that CFTC-regulated derivative exchanges and clearinghouses can count Bitcoin, Ether and payment stablecoins toward meeting their financial resource requirements.

CFTC rules require derivatives exchanges, swap trading venues and clearinghouses to maintain enough financial resources to cover at least 12 months of operating costs on a rolling basis.

The latest staff guidance clarifies that certain crypto assets can count toward part of that requirement, but with a discount to their market value. CFTC staff said they would accept a “haircut” of at least 20% for Bitcoin and Ether and 2% for qualifying payment stablecoins to account for the risk of holding those assets.

The guidance gives CFTC-regulated exchanges and entities more flexibility in how they meet their operating reserve requirements. CFTC-regulated entities include Coinbase Derivatives, Crypto.com’s North American Derivatives Exchange and Bitnomial Exchange, as well as prediction markets Kalshi and Polymarket US.

However, they will still need to meet a separate liquidity requirement with assets such as cash or highly liquid securities.

The advisory represents the views of staff at the Division of Market Oversight and Division of Clearing and Risk, and is not considered a formal rule change approved by the Commission.

#4940. Anchorage Digital Sets Up Asset Manager to Offer Bitcoin Yield to Clients

Anchorage Digital, the first federally chartered crypto bank in the U.S., is moving into asset management with a new subsidiary that will offer custody clients a way to earn yield on their bitcoin.

The unit, called 61st Parallel Asset Management, is expected to start operating by early December, CEO Nathan McCauley said in an interview to CoinDesk. Its first product will be a bitcoin-denominated fund, meaning returns are measured in BTC rather than dollars. The name nods to the city of Anchorage, Alaska, which sits at 61 degrees north latitude.

“We have increasingly heard clients say they want to earn on top of the assets they hold at Anchorage — something that’s very common among the large financial institutions of the world,” McCauley said.

Anchorage has filed a Form ADV, the disclosure document investment advisers use to register with the Securities and Exchange Commission or state regulators, or to report as exempt advisers. The form covers a firm’s ownership, business, assets under management, fees and conflicts of interest. As of Tuesday afternoon, the SEC’s public adviser database showed no record for 61st Parallel, so the filing’s details were not yet public.

The entity itself is not new. New York state records show that 61st Parallel Asset Management LLC, a Delaware company, registered to do business in New York on July 8, listing an office on Park Avenue South in Manhattan.

Anchorage already lets clients earn on some holdings. Its website lists staking, which pays rewards for helping secure proof-of-stake networks, and a separate rewards product for eligible assets. Bitcoin runs on proof-of-work and cannot be staked natively.

Anchorage has not said publicly how the fund will generate yield, what it will charge or which clients will qualify. Those details matter to bitcoin holders, because bitcoin pays no interest on its own. Common ways to earn on it include lending coins out, posting them as collateral or selling options against them, and each carries its own risk.

Public companies have already tested some of those approaches. Trump Media disclosed this month that it had pledged about 73% of its bitcoin to an options program in which the counterparty can rehypothecate, or reuse, the coins.

Founded in 2017, Anchorage received a national trust bank charter from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency in January 2021, the first crypto firm to win one. The OCC lifted a 2022 consent order over the bank’s anti-money laundering controls in August 2025.

The bank no longer stands alone. Last December, the OCC granted conditional approvals to five more digital asset firms, including Circle, Ripple, BitGo, Paxos and Fidelity Digital Assets, to become national trust banks.

The asset manager is the latest in a run of expansions. On Nov. 5, Anchorage Digital Swap Dealer LLC applied to the National Futures Association to register as a swap dealer with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. The company said much of its options growth has come from public companies holding bitcoin and ether on their balance sheets.

In February, Tether made a $100 million strategic investment in Anchorage at a $4.2 billion valuation, after picking Anchorage Digital Bank as the issuer of its U.S. stablecoin. Anchorage also ran its first employee tender offer at that valuation instead of raising new primary capital.

In June, the company rolled out off-exchange settlement with Binance, letting institutions trade on the exchange while their assets stay in segregated custody at the bank. Anchorage also offers trading, staking and settlement to institutional clients.

The swap dealer application remains under review by the National Futures Association, and McCauley said at the time that the company was not in a position to speculate on timing.

#4939. Ethereum Foundation doubles protocol security team ahead of overhaul

The foundation said its next upgrade will be harder than the Merge, and the required pace of development will make it easier to ship bugs.

The Ethereum Foundation says it has doubled its protocol security team as it accelerates work to overhaul Ethereum’s defenses against threats posed by quantum computers and artificial intelligence.

In a Monday blog post, Ethereum Foundation researcher Kev Wedderburn said that while Ethereum has been planning ways to mitigate threats posed by quantum computers, AI has now emerged as a more urgent risk.

The planned overhaul would change how Ethereum validators sign messages, how users authorize transactions and how Ethereum verifies data posted by rollups.

“This upgrade is harder than the Merge, and we have less time,” said Wedderburn, while acknowledging that faster development “makes it easier to ship bugs.”

He said in response, the foundation has expanded its protocol security team to ensure formal verification and security work can keep pace with development.

“Every layer of the protocol and ecosystem will need to adapt to the reality that hardening the protocol is now our highest priority,” he added.

Earlier this month, Ethereum Foundation researcher Justin Drake outlined a December 2028 target for completing Ethereum’s post-quantum and post-AI transition, a year earlier than the foundation’s previously announced quantum-resistance deadline.

Blockchain analytics platform Lookonchain said Tuesday that a suspected attacker had sold memecoins from Ansem's wallet and transferred $2.57 million in USDC to an Arbitrum address. The funds are still parked in that address at the time of publication.

Ansem made a public post on his X account, saying his Pump.fun wallet had been hacked and pointing to a potential breach of his account on Bullpen, a crypto trading platform he cofounded, where he imported his Solana private key.

Pushing back on this, onchain analyst MLM pointed to transactions that occurred before the sell-off.

"The onchain activity looks nothing like a hack," MLM wrote on X. "Just an hour before the selling started, a previously inactive wallet I’d labeled as Ansem’s a year ago funded the wallet that later received the sale proceeds."

Ansem denied being behind the transactions, adding that his theory of a compromised Bullpen account could explain why the alleged attacker could also access other wallets.

"It is not me, would appreciate you not spreading misinformation," Ansem wrote in response to MLM, adding that he was conducting a security audit.

i dont know what the attack vector was, if it was through bullpen then would make sense they have access to other wallets on that account as well, i dont think they have access to the evm pump wallets because those positions are still open and nothing has been moved there it is not me, would appreciate you not spreading misinformation currently doing security audit

Ansem also said he did not believe his EVM-compatible Pump.fun wallets had been compromised because his positions remained open and no funds had been moved.

Ansem's creator coin, The Black Bull (ANSEM), started falling after initial reports of the sell-off, culminating in the coin being down 55% on the day to under $0.02. It's the token's lowest price since launching this past June.

#4936. GTA 6 PC Ports ‘Nuked’ Just Days Before Devs Expected It to Be Playable

GTA 6 PC Ports ‘Nuked’ Just Days Before Devs Expected It to Be Playable

Several major projects attempting to port Grand Theft Auto 6 to PC have been "nuked," according to community insiders. It comes as developers thought a playable port was just days away, after notorious Rockstar hacker Cyberleek released the game's files.

Both the Leonida GitHub page and the GTA6Modding Discord server—two of the most serious attempts at porting the latest Grand Theft Auto title to PC—have been removed. Other servers also involved in the AI-powered porting scene, such as the Chasm Server, have also locked down.

"Leonida and GTA6Modding have both been nuked," Freakman, a Chasm Server mod, wrote on Discord. "We have no affiliation with Cyberleek," they added. "Multiple servers have been struck, we're staying low for tonight."

Cyberleek released an Xbox build of GTA 6 on November 19, the day the game launched on consoles. However, they held back the main executable needed to run it and promised they'd release it if the CYBERLEEK meme coin hit a $15 million market cap.

Porting projects had been preparing for that file, expecting it'd be the key to making the port playable. The scene leans heavily on AI coding tools to speed up the reverse engineering needed to get console games running on PC, with developers describing themselves as "vibe coders."

The meme coin missed its $15 million target, but Cyberleek released the executable on Monday anyway. The next day, several GTA 6 porting projects were shut down.

"They're taking out servers left and right that are mentioning the leak," Chasm community member Weedgoose told Decrypt. "Some servers take the hit while others are going dark and are waiting for the flames to extinguish."

Some of the impacted community members have moved to alternative messaging platforms that are more private than Discord, Weedgoose said.

It appears the Leonida GitHub was removed by its creator, an apparent high school student, as it shows a 404 error page rather than a DMCA takedown page. That said, there's no way of knowing if the creator received a cease and desist (or similar correspondence) that led to this decision.

Chasm mod Freakman did not respond to Decrypt's request for comment regarding why the server has gone dark.

Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar's parent company, has been going after the leaks for months. In August, it filed subpoenas asking Discord and Microsoft, which owns GitHub, to hand over data that could help identify Cyberleek.

Rockstar has yet to announce an official PC version of GTA 6 yet. GamesBeat reported in October that one could arrive in Q1 of 2027—and the prospect of an unofficial port releasing in advance of that would likely dent sales.

Rockstar did not respond to Decrypt's request for comment.

#4935. Google wants to make you the star of your own AI slop movies

Viewers could find their AI-doppelgangers inserted into the crowd during the Cricket World Cup, or take a leading role in their very own romantic comedy.

Google has filed for a patent on a system that uses information it has on you to create a customized AI-generated TV channel, full of shows that star you as the protagonist.

The patent, submitted May 13, 2025, and published by the US Patent and Trademark Office on Thursday, describes a system called “My Channel,” filled with AI-generated content tailored to a user’s watch history and demographic data. The system could use photos or videos of the viewer to create a digital likeness and generate a synthetic voice for their character’s dialogue.

“You are a customized video generating model. Generate a customized video for a user where the user will play the protagonist,” the example AI prompt reads.

“The generated customized video includes characteristics based on the . The generated customized video follows the style and format of the of the user. The generated customized video sticks to the of the user, but the narrative for the generated customized video is customized.”

Many companies file patents that never become products. However, Google’s proposal isn’t too far off from reality. In China, AI-powered filmmakers are generating hundreds of one-minute TV microdramas, called “duanju,” each day.

Related: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO amid ongoing intelligence probe

Shortical, an Israeli-based streaming service available in the US, produces fully AI-generated microdramas among conventional titles. It even allows users to audition their face to be potentially added as characters in future AI-generated microseries.

Google envisions the kinds of genres a user could find themselves starring in. Source: USPTO

In another example, Google describes a user who has recently watched a video about a cricket player in the Cricket World Cup.

“The video should incorporate elements of the Cricket World Cup and Player 1’s recent performance. Perhaps [user_name] could be cheering for India in the stands or interacting with Player 1 in some way,” it wrote.

Google’s proposal also makes room for commercials. In one version described in the filing, when a viewer picks an AI-generated show, an ad server retrieves the video, inserts ads and streams the resulting version to the viewer’s TV.

The application names Aravind Reddy Ayuluri, a software engineer and Prameela Kavya Thummuru, a machine learning engineer at Google as the inventors.

#4933. Robinhood co-leads $5 million seed round for onchain trading platform Rialto

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Tandem, the venture arm of Offchain, the company behind Arbitrum, co-led the round with Robinhood.

Rialto, an onchain trading platform for crypto and tokenized assets, has raised $5 million in a strategic seed round.

Robinhood and Tandem, the venture arm of Arbitrum developer Offchain, co-led the round, Rialto said Tuesday. They were the only investors, Rialto co-founder Can told The Block. Rialto began raising in October 2025 and closed the round in early 2026, Can said. The platform has announced the funding now as it emerged from stealth after a year of development, during which it said it worked closely with Tandem, Offchain and Robinhood.

It was Rialto's first funding round and was structured as equity with token warrants, Can said. He did not disclose the valuation or answer whether Rialto plans to launch a token or raise more funding in the near future.

Can said that is his real first name but declined to disclose his full name. Another co-founder, who goes by Riley, also declined to disclose their full name. Can said most of the Rialto team comes from a high-frequency trading background and has experience building low-latency trading systems.

"That's the experience we're bringing to onchain markets," Can said. "Onchain markets have demonstrated the benefits of transparency and composability, but the next phase requires trading infrastructure that can deliver competitive liquidity and execution at scale."

Rialto offers spot crypto trading and more than 200 Robinhood Stock Tokens on Robinhood Chain. The platform supports tokenized assets linked to equities, ETFs and commodities, and aims to offer deeper liquidity, competitive prices, low fees and better trade execution.

Can said Rialto relies on its proprietary market-making infrastructure and routing technology. "Our PropAMM-driven approach puts market-making and inventory management directly onchain, so professional market makers can quote competitive prices," he said.

Rialto's router looks across trading venues for the best available price, Can said, noting that a recent upgrade cut average quote response times from 250 milliseconds to 20 milliseconds. "Faster quotes track the market more closely, which means tighter prices for traders on the Rialto app and for platforms using the Swap API," he said.

"Bringing onchain assets together with competitive liquidity and fast execution is the kind of work that helps the Robinhood Chain ecosystem grow, and we're excited to back the team," Ben Einstein, director of corporate and business development at Robinhood, said in a statement.

Asked about competitors, Can said Rialto's Swap API competes with aggregators on liquidity and speed on Robinhood Chain, and its app is designed to compete with centralized platforms on performance and fees. Rialto earns revenue from a 5-basis-point trading fee on the app, Can said. He did not share revenue figures.

Rialto reported $199.3 million in trading volume in October, up from $53.4 million in September. Stock token trading volume rose 329% from September to $183.8 million in October, the platform said. Can said Rialto has processed more than $600 million in spot trading volume across its app and Swap API since launching publicly in July 2026.

Asked about expansion to other blockchains, Can said Robinhood Chain remains Rialto's priority, and its Swap API is also live on Arbitrum. He said Rialto is working with firms in both ecosystems to support more assets as they come onchain.

"Our focus is on working with Robinhood and Offchain to make Rialto the go-to place to trade on Robinhood Chain and a core aggregator for Arbitrum," Can said.

"We think the Robinhood Chain has a big opportunity to bring a new class of users onchain, and to give them execution that matches what they're used to on centralized platforms," Can added. "We have no other chains to announce."

Rialto said it will use the funding for product development, hiring, and expansion. Can said the company was founded in mid-2025 and has fewer than 10 people across Europe and Asia, most of them engineers. It is hiring for backend engineering, marketing, and business development.

#4930. Why 42 Macro says it’s waiting to buy the Bitcoin dip

The independent macro research company warns the Bitcoin sell-off may not have yet run its course.

Darius Dale, founder and CEO of 42 Macro, says his firm has trimmed its Bitcoin exposure and is waiting for signs that the sell-off has run its course before it considers buying again.

“We’ve already de-risked out of Bitcoin,” Dale said in an interview with Cointelegraph last week. “Our stress levels are low. We’re just waiting to buy.”

Dale’s comments came just days before Bitcoin fell to a two-year low around $55,100 on Saturday, raising questions about whether Bitcoin has finally found its bottom this cycle.

However, Dale warned that persistently high inflation could prompt further Fed tightening that could drain the liquidity that supports Bitcoin. The US Federal Reserve is widely expected to increase rates by 25 basis points at its next meeting on Dec. 9.

“Bitcoin doesn’t generate earnings. Bitcoin needs liquidity to go up,” he said.

Bitcoin was trading at around $64,000 at the time of the interview. Dale said it could fall another 30% to 40% if the S&P 500’s decline from its Oct. 6 peak reaches 20% by Christmas, which would put it at around $38,400. The S&P500 is currently down 7.4% from that peak.

Related: Bitcoin rebounds 17% from $55K lows as Nvidia rally sparks $500M crypto liquidations

Asked when 42 Macro may consider buying Bitcoin again, Dale said the firm will be looking at its own market signals.

“And once we pivot to a risk on market regime, once Bitcoin, the bottoming process concludes and our signals go from bearish right now to neutral or maybe even back to bullish. That’s when you want to buy.”

Despite near-term caution, Dale expects the conditions to become more favorable for Bitcoin around the middle of 2027, when easing inflation could give the Fed room to shift away from tighter monetary policy.

“So we think 2027 will be a phenomenal year for stocks, gold, Bitcoin,” he said.

Dale said the Fed may need to see second-quarter inflation data before changing course, putting the potential shift in late June or in the first half of the third quarter.

#4929. Morning Minute: Jensen Returns, Markets Soar (Except Crypto)

Morning Minute: Jensen Returns, Markets Soar (Except Crypto)

Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner. The analysis and opinions expressed are his own and do not necessarily reflect those of Decrypt. And check out our daily news show 'FOMO HOUR' covering all of the top stories and market action.

Six days after Nvidia’s board chair told investors “the Nvidia board does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” the board voted unanimously to reinstate him as president, CEO and director, effective immediately.

Nvidia shares rose 33% to around $167, adding roughly a trillion dollars of market value in a session. Huang’s personal net worth climbed about $36.6 billion on his 3.5% stake, moving him to 13th on the Forbes global list. Short sellers took roughly $12.2 billion in paper losses, their worst single day since at least 2019, which wiped out the $10.5 billion they had booked the prior week.

The stock market absolutely ripped on the news. The Nasdaq closed up 6.51% at 24,089, its best day since April 2025. The S&P gained 4.7%, the Dow was +3%, and the VIX collapsed 25.8% to 26.62.

Bitcoin went along with the ride—for a few hours. It touched $63,929 intraday, up 5.1%, then spent the afternoon handing it back and finished near $61,000, barely up on the day. The ETFs used the pump to exit more, with BTC ETFs seeing another $570M in outflows on the day.

ETH and other majors also closed red. Alts gave back their gains. And the CMC top 20 index managed just 0.20% gain.

That’s a 19 to 1 ratio between what the Nasdaq captured and what Bitcoin kept, on the same catalyst, on the same day. Pain for the crypto bulls.

What makes it even more painful, is that crypto fell with AI stocks the whole way down, and the standard explanation was that both trade on the same liquidity and the same risk appetite. Monday tested that and the correlation fell through. The AI trade got a catalyst and markets bounced. Crypto didn’t bounce with it.

As for Nvidia’s reversal decision itself, questions remain to say the least. The board says it was satisfied with Huang’s “candor and ability to lead,” and that input from senior U.S. officials left it confident his return “poses no national security risk.” Trump publicly pushed for it and said the board had sought assurance on the espionage allegations. What actually changed between November 17 and November 23 hasn’t been explained. The independent directors’ investigation is still open, and Nvidia is now standing up a board committee for national security and export-control oversight plus recruiting a chief compliance officer.

Perhaps answers will trickle out over time. The AI trade may not need them anyway. And crypto, well, it's in its own world right now, waiting for its own catalysts (likely quantum-related). But it’s very unclear that catalyst is coming in 2026, and it’s becoming clear that many are not interested in waiting for the answers…

South Korea’s Financial Services Commission (FSC) unveiled a draft bill Tuesday that would initially limit issuance of won-denominated stablecoins to groups majority-owned by banks and generally cap shareholders’ stakes in crypto exchanges at 20%.

Banks would have to own more than half of a stablecoin issuer collectively, though a fintech or technology company could be its largest individual shareholder, the FSC said in its announcement.

Domestic stablecoin issuers would need FSC authorization and at least 5 billion won (about $3.7 million) in equity capital. They would also have to hold reserves covering at least 100% of their outstanding tokens and redeem them at face value without delay.

Exchanges would need dealing, brokerage and custody licenses and would have to meet capital and operating requirements. Shareholders’ stakes would be capped at 20%, or 34% with FSC approval.

The draft also seeks to lift South Korea’s 2017 ban on domestic initial coin offerings.

“Bitcoin doesn’t generate earnings. Bitcoin needs liquidity to go up,” he said.

Bitcoin was trading at around $64,000 at the time of the interview. Dale said it could fall another 30% to 40% if the S&P 500’s decline from its Oct. 6 peak reaches 20% by Christmas, which would put it at around $38,400. The S&P500 is currently down 7.4% from that peak.

Nvidia’s board unanimously voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as president and CEO after consultations with senior US government officials, concluding that his return posed no national security risk despite an ongoing investigation into an alleged foreign intelligence operation targeting him.

In a Monday announcement, Nvidia said its directors were satisfied with Huang’s candor and ability to lead following a series of discussions. The independent investigation will continue despite his reinstatement.

Nvidia shares surged 28.91% to $161.82 shortly after US markets opened on Monday, according to Yahoo Finance data.

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress, who served as interim CEO, will return to her previous role, while Harvey Jones will remain chair of the board.

The chipmaker also said it had recently formed a National Security and Export Control Committee comprising independent directors to oversee compliance and security risks. Nvidia plans to appoint a chief compliance officer and said it would continue cooperating with government investigations.

#4925. Bitcoin Lender Ledn Moves US Clients Onshore With New Custody Accounts

Bitcoin lender Ledn is moving beyond loans. The company launched Ledn Custody on Tuesday, a new account that lets eligible U.S. clients hold bitcoin, gold, stablecoins and U.S. dollars, and buy, sell and swap between them in one place, with no trading fees and a 0.5% spread.

Ledn says that spread makes buying bitcoin through its app about half the cost of a standard purchase on the most popular U.S. bitcoin apps. The launch also moves Ledn’s U.S. clients, previously served from its Cayman Islands entity, to a U.S. company with a U.S. custodian.

Ledn has lent against bitcoin since 2018 and has serviced more than $11 billion in loans. Until now, most of its U.S. clients bought their bitcoin elsewhere and moved it to Ledn to borrow against it. The new account brings that first purchase in-house, from buying through to borrowing.

A standard bitcoin purchase on the most popular U.S. apps costs about 0.9% to 1.25% once trading fees and spread are included, according to Ledn’s own analysis of published fees from October. That puts Ledn in direct competition with the trading apps where many Americans buy their first bitcoin.

On a $1,000 purchase, that works out to about $5 at Ledn against $9 to $12.50 elsewhere. Clients can deposit dollars and hold them in the account, or use them to buy bitcoin, gold and stablecoins. BitGo describes the gold option as tokenized gold.

“What our clients want is to hold hard assets, whether that’s bitcoin, gold or stablecoins,” Ledn co-founder and Chief Strategy Officer Mauricio Di Bartolomeo said. “Most people buy them in one place, keep them in another, and when they need cash, they sell. Now they can do all three in one account.”

He added that clients can borrow against their bitcoin instead of selling, “with gold to follow.”

Assets in a Ledn Custody account are held for the benefit of each client by an independent qualified custodian, segregated from Ledn’s own assets and never lent out for interest. BitGo Bank & Trust, a unit of BitGo (BTGO), provides the custody and trading services behind the account.

The custody setup is a selling point for a lender that came through 2022. Ledn says it has returned every client’s collateral across two full market cycles, including the collapse that bankrupted Celsius, BlockFi and Voyager. The company has also published monthly loan book and proof of reserves data.

“We’ve spent eight years earning our clients’ trust as a lender,” Ledn co-founder and CEO Adam Reeds said. “If you’re going to be a financial services company, boring is a good thing. We want to be the reliable, stable place where people build their wealth, not a platform with a million features built for trading.”

The onshore move lines up with Washington’s message. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in May that crypto’s problems stem from “the wild, wild west offshore,” adding, “we got to bring it onshore.” The Clarity Act, the market structure bill he urged Congress to pass, stalled in the Senate in September.

Ledn is chasing a big market. More than 67 million Americans now own crypto, or about one in four U.S. adults, according to a May survey. Competition for bitcoin borrowers is also heating up, with Cross River Bank launching its first bitcoin-backed loans this week.

Ledn has leaned on the capital markets to fund its lending, selling $188 million in bitcoin-backed bonds in February. The custody account now gives the lender a way to win clients before they ever need a loan.

Ledn Custody accounts will roll out to eligible U.S. individual clients over the coming days. The company plans to add lending against gold and open more U.S. states in the coming weeks.

#4923. CertiK Trains Interpol Investigators to Trace and Freeze Stolen Crypto

CertiK Trains Interpol Investigators to Trace and Freeze Stolen Crypto

Blockchain security firm CertiK trained police investigators from across Asia and the South Pacific in tracing stolen crypto and securing asset freezes at an INTERPOL meeting in Hanoi, the company said.

The 3rd INTERPOL Asia and South Pacific Working Group Meeting on Cybercrime ran from October 27 to October 30, 2026. It was organized by INTERPOL's Cybercrime Directorate and Vietnam's Ministry of Public Security. CertiK said senior law enforcement officials from 20 countries attended, with stablecoin issuer Tether and South Korean exchange Upbit among the other private-sector partners.

CertiK's sessions focused on the two stages of recovering stolen crypto: mapping how funds move after a theft, then using that evidence to ask exchanges to freeze them.

Officers worked through a real wallet-compromise case, using open-source block explorers and CertiK's compliance software to follow stolen funds through token swaps, cross-chain bridges and intermediary wallets to three deposit addresses at an exchange. The exercise included spotting address-poisoning decoys, which attackers use to send investigators down false trails.

CertiK's team then explained the process for contacting the exchange, using its law enforcement portal and filing formal requests to freeze the funds.

Other sessions covered how to read wallet activity before and after a suspicious transaction, how smart contract vulnerabilities and audit findings can inform an investigation, and how to tell apart attacks involving compromised signing keys, phishing and social engineering.

"Investigators need both a clear picture of how an attack happened and a practical route to act on the evidence," Esme Pau, CertiK's head of capital markets and policy, said in a statement.

Fellow security firm Group-IB, which also presented, tweeted that the four-day meeting drew more than 80 participants from over 43 countries and regions. INTERPOL's working group for heads of regional cybercrime units first met in Manila in September 2024.

The training comes as INTERPOL steps up its work on crypto-enabled crime. In July 2026, it said that a 20-year-old Thai suspect's wallet had moved more than $122.5 million in romance-scam proceeds in 10 months, using cross-chain swaps to hide the trail. The case was one of many in Operation First Light, a 97-country sweep that led to 5,811 arrests.
